persona.name: Anjali Gupta
persona.background: She runs a small shop in Delhi and spends long hours at work, often under stress. She reports that her skin problems tend to flare during stressful periods.

diagnoses.name: Plaque psoriasis (psoriasis vulgaris), chronic plaque psoriasis
diagnoses.description: Noninfectious, chronic papulosquamous, T-cell-mediated inflammatory disorder with well-defined pink-red sharply demarcated plaques covered by silvery scales; extensor surfaces and scalp are typical; Auspitz sign and grattage test may be positive.

diagnoses.name: Atopic dermatitis (atopic eczema)
diagnoses.description: Endogenous eczema with extremely itchy erythematous scaly patches; acute lesions may have small vesicles and severe cases show weeping/crusting; chronic rubbing causes lichenification; flexor distribution is typical.

diagnoses.name: Seborrheic dermatitis
diagnoses.description: Erythematous scaling affecting nasolabial folds, eyebrows, eyelids, and glabella; scalp dandruff is common; may involve external auditory canal and postauricular areas.

diagnoses.name: Pityriasis versicolor (tinea versicolor)
diagnoses.description: Persistent superficial infection by Malassezia furfur causing round/oval scaly macules on upper trunk (often hypopigmented on dark skin, sometimes hyperpigmented on light skin); confirmed by scraping with 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance.

diagnoses.name: Erythema multiforme
diagnoses.description: Acute self-limiting recurrent cutaneous/mucocutaneous eruption with target-shaped plaques; lesions are symmetrical, acral and centripetal (extremities > face > neck > trunk); may follow herpes infection.

diagnoses.name: Lichen planus
diagnoses.description: Pruritic planar purple polygonal papules/plaques (the '5 P’s'), often on flexor surfaces (especially wrists); may show Wickham’s striae and Koebner phenomenon; oral mucosal involvement can occur.

diagnoses.name: Vitiligo
diagnoses.description: Slowly progressive acquired focal loss of melanocytes causing well-circumscribed depigmented macules/patches, often around body orifices and on hands/feet; may show Koebner phenomenon; patients are very susceptible to sunburn.

diagnoses.name: Pityriasis alba
diagnoses.description: Hypopigmented patches or macules with slight scale mainly on the face (less often neck/trunk/extremities), often in children and with a history of atopy; improves after puberty.

diagnoses.name: Stevens–Johnson syndrome
diagnoses.description: Rare, acute, life-threatening mucocutaneous disease nearly always drug-related with erythematous dusky red atypical targetoid macules that coalesce and evolve into flaccid blisters with epidermal detachment (<10% BSA); mucosa normally involves at least two sites.

diagnoses.name: Bullous pemphigoid
diagnoses.description: Autoimmune blistering disorder typically in elderly; itchy tense bullae with negative Nikolsky sign; mucosal involvement in 10–30%.

initialComplaint: For the last 2 days, I suddenly developed red ‘ring-like’ spots on my hands and feet that seem to be spreading upward.
medicalHistory: She reports a preceding herpetic infection before the skin eruption. No other past history provided.
symptoms:
Acute onset of a multiforme eruption with macules, papules, vesicles and bullae. Lesions are target-shaped plaques. Distribution is symmetrical, acral and centripetal with extensor aspect involvement (extremities more than face, then neck and trunk).

The distribution (hands/feet with centripetal spread) and morphology (target plaques) do not match the typical **tense bullae/urticarial plaques** pattern of bullous pemphigoid.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **Age group** - Bullous pemphigoid usually affects **>60**; **erythema multiforme** often affects younger patients.
**Time course** - Bullous pemphigoid is **chronic/relapsing**; **erythema multiforme** is typically **acute** and self-limited.
**Primary lesion morphology** - Bullous pemphigoid features **tense bullae/urticarial plaques**; **erythema multiforme** features **target lesions** with concentric zones.
**Symptoms** - Bullous pemphigoid is characteristically **itchy**; **erythema multiforme** is more often burning/tender and may follow infection.
**Distribution** - Bullous pemphigoid commonly involves trunk/flexures; **erythema multiforme** is **acral** with **centripetal** spread and extensor predominance.
**Etiologic association** - Bullous pemphigoid is autoimmune (**BP180/BP230**); **erythema multiforme** is commonly **herpes-associated**.
missingFindings: **Elderly onset** - Typical presentation is in patients >60; young age makes bullous pemphigoid unlikely.
**Predominant pruritus** - Marked itching is expected; case emphasizes target lesions and acute spread instead.
**Tense widespread bullae** - Classic firm bullae are not the dominant described lesion morphology here.
**Urticarial prebullous phase** - Often precedes bullae in bullous pemphigoid; not described in this case.
**Supportive autoimmune evidence** - No mention of **BP180/BP230** antibodies or subepidermal blistering on biopsy.

differentialDiagnoses.name: Stevens–Johnson syndrome (SJS)
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: SJS is nearly always drug-related and is characterized by <10% BSA detachment; mucous membranes normally involve at least two sites, and lesions are described as erythematous, dusky red, flat, atypical targetoid macules that can progress to flaccid blisters and epidermal detachment.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “SJS… nearly always drug-related… ‘minor form of TEN’ with <10% body surface area (BSA) detachment… [mucous membrane] normally involves at least two sites… evolve into flaccid blisters… Detachment of epidermis.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN)
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: TEN has >30% BSA detachment and no target lesions; Nikolsky sign often positive; begins with severe mucosal erosions and progresses to generalized detachment.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “TEN… Detachment of >30% BSA… Nikolsky sign often positive… No target lesions seen… begins with severe mucosal erosions and progresses to diffuse, generalized detachment.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Pemphigus vulgaris
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Pemphigus vulgaris is chronic/relapsing with painful lesions, common mucosal involvement, flaccid bullae (often ruptured), and positive Nikolsky sign—features not typical of EM target lesions and acute self-limiting course.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Pemphigus vulgaris… Chronic, relapsing… Painful… Mucosal involvement Common… Bullae Flaccid… Nikolsky sign Positive.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Bullous pemphigoid
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Bullous pemphigoid typically affects elderly, is itchy, has tense bullae, mucosal involvement only 10–30%, and Nikolsky sign negative—distinguishing it from EM with target lesions and typical acral distribution.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Bullous pemphigoid… Elderly >60… Itchy… Bullae Tense… Mucosal involvement 10–30%… Nikolsky sign Negative.”

idealPathway.diagnosticApproach: Diagnose erythema multiforme clinically by identifying the characteristic target lesions (three concentric zones, sometimes with central bulla/crust) and the typical distribution (symmetrical, acral, centripetal; extensor predominance; extremities > face > neck > trunk; sun-exposed/Koebnerization). Classify as EM minor (cutaneous without mucosal involvement) versus EM major (cutaneous plus mucosal involvement), noting oral mucosal lesions are usually absent or few and mildly symptomatic when present. Elicit precipitating factors—especially preceding herpetic infection (~50%), other infections (including Mycoplasma), and drug exposures (e.g., sulfonamides, penicillins, barbiturates, salicylates, hydantoins, antimalarials, carbamazepine). Assess for associated features such as malaise and tender, slightly enlarged lymphadenopathy. If systemic involvement is suspected, evaluate organ involvement as described (liver, kidney, lung with CXR/CT findings). Differentiate from SJS/TEN by extent of epidermal detachment, mucosal involvement patterns, and the presence/absence of target lesions (TEN: no target lesions), and from pemphigus vulgaris/bullous pemphigoid using chronicity, symptoms, bulla characteristics, mucosal involvement frequency, and Nikolsky sign.
